name: Pectus bell

lead: The pectus bell, or vacuum bell, is a bowl-shaped device that fits over the depressed area of the chest in pectus excavatum. A hand pump removes air and the vacuum lifts the sternum outward.

The payoff is a flatter or fuller-looking chest, shown to lift the sternum while worn. Studies report lasting correction in some patients, with better results in younger people with shallow, flexible defects.

paras: The cup is worn over the sunken area for set periods, often alongside physiotherapy exercises, over many months. Some surgeons also use it as preparation for surgery or to lift the sternum during the Nuss procedure.

Reported effects include temporary skin marks and discomfort from suction. Clinical sources describe it as an option for selected, flexible cases rather than a substitute for surgery in all patients; a pectus specialist can assess suitability.

chain: Depression reduces over months of use with exercise
angle.text: The device lifts the sunken sternum immediately while worn, and in flexible chests repeated use is reported to give lasting improvement in how the chest looks.

lead: A vacuum bell is a non-surgical treatment for pectus excavatum, a sunken-chest deformity. A bowl-shaped device sits over the depression and a hand pump creates a vacuum that lifts the sternum [1].

It helps looks directly while worn by raising the chest wall, and with continued use may produce lasting correction. It was described in a 2006 paper by Haecker and Mayr as a potential alternative to surgery [1][2].
Pectus defects occur in roughly 1 in 250 people; most are well tolerated, but some young people experience lower self-esteem and avoid activities such as swimming [3].

paras: The cup is applied over the sunken area and evacuated with a pump so the sternum rises [1]. It is used with physiotherapy exercises, and is also used to prepare patients for surgery [1]. In a randomized trial of 26 boys aged 11 to 18, one group used the bell alone and another added a physiotherapy program [4].
The method was described in 2006 [1][2]. A 2012 press release reported the first U.S. patients receiving the device [1].

A single-center study found excellent correction in 20% of patients; the authors said it is not a substitute for the Nuss procedure, which they reported gives excellent results in 90% [1]. Predictors of excellent outcome included age 11 or under, chest wall depth of 1.5 cm or less, flexibility and 12 consecutive months of use [1]. A 2025 systematic review of 20 pediatric studies assessed the probability of success [5]. Practice guidelines and reviews place it among options for selected patients [3][6].
Surgeons have used the bell intraoperatively to lift the sternum during the Nuss procedure [7].

The studies above include a 2006 initial report [2], a randomized trial of physiotherapy added to vacuum bell therapy [4], a 2025 systematic review [5], and a clinical trial of the immediate sternal lift from short use [7]. A 2024 UK consensus guideline covers pectus care generally [3].
